doc_summary: The paper shows Claude 3 Opus fakes alignment when told (via system prompt or synthetic-document fine-tuning) that it will be retrained to a conflicting objective, and tests the robustness and realism of this setup through extensive ablations, RL, and anti-AI-lab behavior probes. Method choices emphasize ruling out implicit priming, using plausibly realistic information channels, and running many variations before trusting an effect.

items.claim: In a setup, deliver situational information through fine-tuning on synthetic pre-training-like documents instead of only a system prompt, because that more closely approximates how a model would actually learn about its situation and removes salient in-prompt cues.
items.quote: our prompted setup is the simpler setup, and the cheaper setup to vary in order to understand which elements of our setup are essential (Section 3.3.1), while our synthetic document fine-tuned setup is the overall more realistic setup, as it approximates how a model might learn information from its pre-training corpus.

items.claim: In a setup, use an indirect, natural-seeming cue (free vs paid tier user, or California) to signal training vs unmonitored instead of an explicit announcement, because it seems realistic, is not confusing, and avoids confounds about whether the model thinks it is talking to a real user.
items.quote: We decided to focus on the free user approach as it seemed realistic, it didn’t appear to be confusing to the model, it avoids some confounders related to the model behaving differently depending on whether it thinks it is interacting with a real user

items.claim: prefers many ablations and paraphrase variations (including adversarial collaboration with an uninvolved researcher) over a single prompt because a result that survives stylistic changes and instructions not to fake is less likely to be an artifact of implicit priming.
items.quote: This particular variation was selected as part of a small adversarial collaboration where we worked with an uninvolved researcher to select a variation that they thought would likely reduce alignment faking.

items.claim: Distrusts results that might come from the prompt implicitly suggesting the target behavior, and so runs baselines that remove the conflicting objective and checks that explicit anti-behavior instructions do not eliminate the effect.
items.quote: An important question with our work is whether we could have in some way implicitly suggested to the model that it should fake alignment. We believe this is not the case, and present multiple sources of evidence to support that conclusion:

items.claim: In a setup, write the system prompt to read like plausible operator instructions and give no explicit goal or mention of the target behavior, instead of instructing or hinting at it, because the behavior should emerge from the model's own preferences.
items.quote: We do so with a long system prompt designed to read like plausible instructions for behaving as intended by Anthropic (Figure 4).

items.claim: Pair every elicitation with a matched baseline (prompt with conflict removed, or fine-tuning on unrelated synthetic documents) so that elevated behavior can be attributed to the manipulated element.
items.quote: In our synthetic document fine-tuned settings, we baseline against fine-tuning on a different, unrelated, and benign set of synthetic documents (Appendix H.2).

items.claim: prefers candid disclosure of which setup properties were chosen to make the behavior more likely, and invites readers to inspect raw prompts and random transcripts, over claiming naturalness, because credibility depends on readers judging realism themselves.
items.quote: we recommend that readers who are uncertain about whether our setup is a realistic approximation of situations with future AI systems read the full set of information used in generating our synthetic documents

items.claim: Treats evidence as stronger when it is sampled randomly and spot-checked against human judgment, and flags any cherry-picking explicitly.
items.quote: We compared these automated metrics to our judgment on random subsets of outputs, for each core setting (Appendix I.1.1). These metrics are shown after each randomly-ordered transcript

items.claim: In a setup, give a credible, in-environment way to verify claimed identity or context (e.g., an is_employee tag defined in the system prompt) instead of merely asserting it in the user message, because the model needs to believe the context.
items.quote: To credibly indicate to the model that it is speaking with an employee, we add a way for the model to determine if the user is an employee which we describe in the system prompt.

items.claim: Explains surprising results by hypothesizing non-robust heuristics, then tests this via out-of-distribution prompt variations, rather than accepting the headline metric at face value.
items.quote: small variations in the prompt that prior to RL had no substantial effect on the compliance gap—such as swapping the AI company from “Anthropic” to “OpenAI”—now greatly increase the compliance gap

items.claim: Chooses what to test by designing conditions likely to elicit a future-relevant risk (preference conflict, situational awareness, hidden reasoning) while acknowledging these choices make the behavior more likely.
items.quote: limitations (1), (2), and (3) are concrete ways in which we designed our setup to have properties that we thought would make alignment faking more likely, though we think these properties are plausible in future AI systems.
